summary: This unit teaches you to write the reports a Level 3 electrician is trusted with: certificates and schedules of test results, condition reports, fault, incident, commissioning, progress and recommendation reports. You will learn to agree the scope, record readings accurately with their units, class defects by danger, separate fact from opinion, use tables, charts and photos, and write clear recommendations. You will also learn to check, sign, hand over and store reports so that they can be relied on years later.

blocks.p: A wiring job is not finished until its paperwork is right. The client cannot see inside a wall or a board: the report is how they know what was done, what was found and whether the installation is safe. Inspectors, insurers, other electricians and sometimes a court will rely on what you wrote. At Level 3 you write these reports yourself, check the ones your team writes, and put your name to them.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Choose the right kind of report
Know when the job needs a certificate, a condition report, a fault, incident, commissioning or progress report, or a short recommendation report.
Agree the purpose, the reader and the scope before the work starts, and note the limitations.
Record readings at the time they are taken, with units and instrument details; take labelled photos; collect statements and documents.
Use a standard structure: details, summary, scope, findings, conclusions, recommendations and appendices, with numbered pages.
Class defects and give a result
Class each defect by how dangerous it is, give an overall result and set time limits for repairs.
Use plain words, exact locations, correct units and dates; separate facts from opinions; report your own team's mistakes.
Use tables, bar charts, line graphs, sketches and captioned photos, each referred to in the text.
Check every figure against the site record, have someone else read the report, sign only for what you are responsible for, and control revisions.
Explain the report to the client in person, keep it confidential, and file copies where they are safe and can be found.

ul: Jamaica's electrical code is based on the US National Electrical Code (NEC). A new or altered installation must be inspected and certified before JPS will connect it. This is overseen by the Government Electrical Regulator, and the inspection is done by a licensed electrical inspector. Your test records and drawings are what the inspector asks to see.

Firms and training centres use their own forms for certificates, schedules of test results and condition reports. Many are modelled on British forms, which is where terms such as 'condition report', 'minor works certificate' and the danger classes in this kit come from. **Use the forms your firm, the Centre or the client specifies**, and learn the ideas behind them: they are the same on every form.
Money is in J$. Where a report gives prices, say whether GCT is included.

blocks.note: A report is a legal record. Never sign for a test you did not do or supervise, and never write a reading you did not take.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Kinds of report and what each is for

head: Report
When it is used
What it must show
rows: **Installation certificate** with its **schedule of test results**
That the work was designed, installed, inspected and tested, and is safe to put into service. Signed for each part.
A small addition or change to one existing circuit, such as an extra outlet or a moved light
What was done, the tests on that circuit, and that the change has not made the circuit unsafe.
An existing installation: is it still safe to use?
Scope and limitations, observations classed by danger, an overall result, recommendations and the date of the next inspection, with test results.
New plant, such as a pump control panel, a generator or a solar system, being set to work
That it works as designed: equipment details, dead tests, settings, function tests, outstanding items and handover.
After a breakdown or a repeated fault is found and repaired
The complaint, the tests, the cause, the repair, the retest and how to stop it happening again.
Someone was hurt, or property was damaged
What happened, in time order, with facts, causes and actions.
Nobody was hurt, but someone could have been
The same as an incident report: it shows a weakness that can be fixed before anyone is hurt.
Weekly or monthly on a longer job
Work done against the plan, problems and their causes, decisions needed and next period's work.
The client must choose between solutions
The problem, the facts, each option with cost, time and risk, and your recommendation.
Work done, people on site, visitors, instructions, deliveries, weather, switching times and problems.

blocks.h: Match the report to the request

ul: A client who asks only whether one new circuit is safe needs a short certificate with its test results, not a long report on the whole building.
A client who asks whether a 25-year-old installation is still safe needs a condition report.
A phone call or a text saying 'all good' is never a report. If the question is about safety, the answer goes in writing.

head: Reader
What they want
rows: Is it safe? What must be done, how soon and at what cost?
Evidence: readings, instruments, who did what, signatures.
What is installed, how it was set and tested, what was left to do.
Insurers and lawyers, after a loss
Exact facts, dates, times and who was responsible.

blocks.note: Write for the reader who knows least. A hotel manager should understand the first page without help; the technical detail goes after it and in the appendices, for the readers who need it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning: purpose, reader, scope and limitations

blocks.p: Ten minutes of planning saves hours of rewriting. Before you go to site, answer four questions: **Why** is the report wanted? **Who** will read it? **What** does it cover? **When** is it needed?

The **scope** says exactly what the report covers: which buildings, boards and circuits, which inspections and tests, and what is left out. It is **agreed with the client before the work starts**, in writing, because it sets the price, the time, the shutdowns needed and what you are responsible for. Ask for old drawings, certificates and earlier reports at the same time.

A **limitation** is anything inside the scope that you could not inspect or test, with the reason: a locked room, a roof space with no safe access, a circuit that could not be switched off, a cable hidden in the structure. Limitations are listed in their own section. You do not guess about what you did not see: you do not call it satisfactory, and you do not call it dangerous.

head: Poor
Better
rows: Store room 2 was locked and the key holder was away; the circuits inside were not inspected or tested.
The roof space above the kitchen has no safe access; wiring there was not inspected.
Circuit 9 (server room) could not be switched off; it was inspected but not tested. A test should be arranged.

flow: Agree the purpose, scope, date and shutdown times with the client, in writing
Collect drawings, earlier certificates and reports
Choose the form or template and prepare blank schedules
Check the instruments: in calibration, leads sound, serial numbers noted
Share the circuits and tasks among the team and brief them on how to record
Do the work and record as you go
Write, check, sign, issue and file

sections.title: Gathering evidence and recording test results

blocks.p: Write each reading on the schedule **as it is taken**, against the right circuit. Readings written up from memory at the end of the day are easily forgotten, swapped between circuits or 'tidied'. If you use a tester that stores readings, still note which stored number belongs to which circuit.
The **schedule of test results** is the table that lists every circuit with its details and its test readings. A typical one has:

head: Column
What goes in it
rows: Size and type of the conductors
Each reading in megohms, with the test voltage: '>200 MΩ at 500 V'
Trip time in milliseconds where the instrument gives it: '24 ms'; test-button result
Anything unusual, a failed first test, a limitation

ul: **Every reading has its unit.** '200' means nothing: 200 Ω and 200 MΩ are a million times apart.
Write the reading **exactly as the instrument shows it**. Do not round 0.38 Ω to 0.4 Ω, and do not guess the last figure.
If the instrument shows that the reading is above its range, record that: **'>999 MΩ'** (more than 999 MΩ). Do not write 'infinite', and do not drop the 'more than' sign.
If a test could not be done, write **'not tested'** and the reason. Never leave a blank, and never copy a reading from a similar circuit.
If a circuit **fails**, mark it clearly, do not energise it, find and repair the fault, then retest. Keep **both** results on the record, with a note of the repair made in between.
Record the **instrument**: its type, serial number and calibration due date. This traces every result to an instrument that was itself checked against a known standard.
Compare each reading with the limit in the specification or the tables, and say whether it passes.

head: Fact (what you saw, measured or did)
Opinion (what you think)
rows: The cable sheath is cut 300 mm from the box.
The cable was probably damaged by rats.
Board DB2 has no circuit chart.
Insulation resistance, line to earth, circuit 6: 0.3 MΩ.
The cable must be wet somewhere.

blocks.p: Opinions have a place: a client pays for your judgement. But mark them as opinions ('In my opinion…', 'The likely cause is…') and give the facts they rest on. Never present a guess as a fact.

ul: **Photos**: take them before anything is moved or repaired, close enough to show the fault, with a label or rule in the picture. Note where each was taken.
**Statements**: after an incident, speak to each person separately and soon, and write down what they say in their own words.
**Documents**: drawings, earlier certificates, makers' data, the trip log or logbook, delivery notes.
**Site notes**: dates, times, who was present, what was switched off and on.

head: Part
What it holds
rows: Report title and number, client, address, date of the work, who did it, revision number.
Half a page at most: the overall result, the urgent items, the main recommendation and, where asked, the cost. Written last, placed first.
Why the report was asked for, and by whom.
What was covered, what was not, and why.
The inspections and tests done, and the instruments used.
The facts: what was found, where, with readings, photos and tables.
What the findings mean: causes, and whether the installation is satisfactory.
What should be done, by when, in order of urgency.
Schedules of test results, calculations, data sheets, the full set of photos.
Who wrote it and who checked it.

ul: Put the **report number and 'page 3 of 15'** on every page, so pages cannot be lost or mixed with another report.
Number the sections and the items in the findings, so a recommendation can point back to its finding ('see item 7').

Keep findings, conclusions and recommendations apart. A sentence such as 'the GFCI tripped 12 times' is a finding; 'the fryer element is leaking current to earth' is a cause; 'replace the element' is a recommendation.
Bulky detail goes in an appendix: the reader of the main text gets the key results, and the full table is there for anyone who needs it.

blocks.p: On a condition report every defect is given a class, so that the client knows how quickly to act. The usual classes are:

head: Class
Meaning
Example
Action
rows: A risk of injury exists now
An outlet with a broken cover and live parts that can be touched
Make it safe before you leave, and tell the client at once, in writing
Not dangerous at this moment, but would become so if another fault happened
A metal light fitting whose earth conductor is not connected
Not dangerous, but fixing it would make the installation safer or easier to use
A missing or out-of-date circuit chart in an otherwise sound board
Something could not be confirmed and needs more work to decide
A reading that suggests a hidden fault

ul: If **any** item is classed as danger present or potentially dangerous, the overall result is **unsatisfactory**, however many other items passed.
If there are only improvement items, the result can be **satisfactory**.
The report also states when the next inspection is due, as the client's type of building and the standard require.

blocks.note: A count of passes does not decide the result. One exposed live conductor in a school makes the report unsatisfactory, even if every other item is perfect.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Writing clearly: words, numbers and recommendations

ul: Use short sentences and everyday words. Explain a technical term the first time, or leave it for the appendix.
Prefer the active voice: 'We replaced the cracked outlet in Room 4', not 'Replacement of the outlet was effected'.
Say exactly **where**: board, circuit number, room, and distance from a fixed point.
No slang, no jokes, no blame, no exclamation marks.

head: Weak
Strong
rows: Lighting circuit was messed up upstairs.
Circuit 3 (first-floor lights): loose line terminal in the junction box above Room 12.
The earth wire to the kitchen outlets is not connected, so a fault could make metal parts live.
The breaker tripped because rain was entering the outdoor box past a missing seal.
Replace the cracked outlet in Room 4 within 7 days.

blocks.p: A **symptom** is what the client notices: the breaker trips, the lights flicker. A **cause** is what makes it happen: water in a box, a loose neutral, a failing element. A fault report that stops at the symptom has not done its job. If you could not prove the cause, say so, and say what you think is most likely, as an opinion.

head: Rule
Right
Wrong
rows: Leave a space between the number and the unit
Use the correct symbol and capital letters: they change the meaning
Symbols take no 's' and no full stop
Write dates so they cannot be misread
Keep the figures the instrument gave

blocks.h: Sums you will meet in reports

ul: **Percentage:** part ÷ whole × 100. If 21 of 24 circuits passed, 21 ÷ 24 × 100 = 87.5% passed.
**How many times larger:** new ÷ old. An insulation reading that rises from 0.5 MΩ to 150 MΩ after a repair is 150 ÷ 0.5 = 300 times larger.
**Percentage points:** when both figures are already percentages, subtract them. A job planned to be 40% complete that is 32% complete is **8 percentage points** behind plan.
**Time:** an inspection due every 3 years is due every 36 months.
Work every sum twice, and show the figures you used so the reader can check them.

blocks.p: A recommendation is advice the client can act on. Each one says **what** to do, **where**, **how soon**, and, where useful, who should do it and what it will cost. List the most urgent first: exposed live parts come before a rusty door or a missing label.

ul: Report what you found, even when the fault is in work your own team did. State the facts, including your team's part.
Keep failed readings on the record with the repair and the retest.
If data is missing, say so. Do not fill gaps with guesses, and do not leave awkward results out of a chart.
Do not soften a danger to please a client, and do not exaggerate one to win work.

head: You want to show
Use
Example
rows: Insulation readings for 24 circuits: circuit, reading, result
A comparison between a few items
kWh used in the month before and the month after new LED lights; trips counted for each circuit
Earth electrode resistance measured each month for a year; planned and actual progress week by week
A pie chart (only for a few slices)
Share of a building's energy use taken by air-conditioning, lighting and other loads

ul: Give every table and chart a number and a title: 'Table 2: Insulation resistance by circuit'.
Put units in the column headings or on the axes: 'Insulation resistance (MΩ)'.
Label both axes of a chart, start the scale where it will not mislead, and add a key if there is more than one set of bars or lines.
Refer to each one in the text and say what it shows: 'Table 1 shows that use fell by about 30%.'
Mention anything else that could explain the figures, such as school holidays in an energy comparison.

blocks.h: From a log to a chart: worked example

blocks.p: A shop's two-week trip log lists 16 trips. Tally them by circuit first:

Check that the tally adds up to the number of entries in the log (2 + 11 + 3 = 16). A bar chart with one bar for each circuit shows at a glance that circuit 5 is the problem. A second tally, by time of day, may show when it trips, which points towards the cause.

ul: Every drawing, chart and photo is a **figure**, numbered in order, with a factual caption: 'Figure 3: scorched terminal, DB1 way 4'.
Take a wide shot to show where, and a close-up to show what. Put a rule or a label in the close-up.
After an incident, where it is safe, photograph the scene **before anything is moved**: it shows the conditions exactly as they were.
A simple sketch often explains a wiring fault better than a paragraph or a photo of the outside of a box.
Do not photograph people, or a client's private property, without need, and keep the photos with the job file, not on social media.

sections.title: Fault, incident, commissioning, progress and recommendation reports

flow: Details: client, address, date, who did the work
The complaint, in the client's own words
Checks and tests done, with readings, units and instruments
The cause, not just the symptom
The repair made
The retest readings showing that it now passes
Recommendations and any follow-up date

blocks.p: The client sees what was wrong and that it is fixed; the firm has a record if the fault returns.

ul: Give the date, time and exact place, and the names of those involved and of witnesses.
Set out what happened **in the order it happened, with times**, as facts.

Record the injury, the first aid given and the medical check. Anyone who has had an electric shock, however small, is reported, recorded and checked by a doctor, because effects on the heart can appear later.
Record the controls: which **PPE was worn** and **how the circuit was isolated** (which switch, lock and tag, proved dead or not). This shows whether the controls worked or failed.
Give the immediate cause and the root cause: not 'he was careless' but 'the wrong breaker was switched off; no lock was fitted; the board was not proved dead'.
List the actions agreed, each with a **named owner and a date**.
Sign and date it, and send it to the people your firm's or the Centre's procedure names.

blocks.p: A **near miss**, such as a tester showing a 'dead' circuit to be live, is reported in the same way. Nobody is being put in trouble: the report exposes a weakness while it can still be fixed for free.

head: Part
Why it matters
rows: So the report can be traced to the right equipment.
Equipment list with makers' details and serial numbers
For warranty claims and spare parts.
Shows it was safe to energise.
Settings made: overloads, timers, level switches, protection
Anyone servicing it later knows how it was set.
Function tests: starts, stops, direction, alarms, trips
Shows it works as designed. Live tests are done by an authorised person.
Manuals and drawings handed over; staff shown how to operate it
The client can run and maintain it.

ul: Job name, week number, date, writer.
Work completed this period **against the plan**: 'Ground floor first fix 100%; first floor 60% (plan 80%).'
Delays, stated plainly, with their cause and their effect on the finish date.
What the team did to recover, and the options, with their cost.
Changes asked for by the client, and whether they have been approved in writing.
Decisions you need from the reader.
Safety: incidents and near misses.
Work planned for the next period.

blocks.note: Send a progress report on time, even when the news is bad. A manager told early can act; a manager told late can only pay.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When a client must choose between solutions, describe each option under the **same headings**: the work needed, how it solves the problem, the cost in J$ (saying whether GCT at the current rate is included), the time and shutdown needed, and the risks. A side-by-side table helps:

head: Heading
Option A: repair the old standby generator
Option B: replace it
rows: New alternator bearings and a new controller
New set of the same rating; reuse the transfer switch
Engine is 18 years old; parts are hard to find

blocks.p: End with a conclusion that says which option best meets the client's needs, and why, based on the facts. Calculations and readings go in an appendix.

sections.title: Checking, signing, handing over and keeping records

ul: Every circuit on the schedule has **all** its readings, each with its unit, or 'not tested' with a reason.
Circuit numbers match the board and the site sheets. If two have been swapped, **correct them, check the rest, then issue**.
Sums, totals and percentages have been worked twice.
Names, dates, the address and the report number are right on every page.
Every figure and table is numbered and mentioned in the text.
Spelling and grammar have been checked, by eye as well as by the computer.
Someone else has read it. The best test of your recommendations is to **ask a person like the reader what they would do** after reading them.

blocks.p: An installation certificate has separate signatures for the **design**, the **installation** and the **inspection and testing**, because different people may have done each part. Each person signs only for their own part and takes responsibility for it. Tests done by an apprentice are signed for by the competent person who supervised and is responsible for them.

If a report is corrected after it has been issued, give it a **new revision number and date**, note what changed, send it to everyone who received the first one and mark the old one as replaced. Two different reports with the same number cause arguments later.

flow: Give the client the signed certificate or report with its schedules, drawings and manuals
Explain in person the main findings and any action they must take
Show them how to switch off in an emergency and how to test the RCDs or GFCIs
Tell them what is outstanding and when the next inspection is due
Ask them to sign that they received the documents
File the firm's copies

ul: The **client** keeps the original; the firm keeps a **copy in the job file**, with the site sheets, photos and handover receipt.
Electronic reports are saved to the **firm's system, which is backed up**: not only on a tablet, a phone or a personal email account.
Keep records for as long as your firm's rules and the law require, often many years. They show that the work was tested properly if there is a later fault, claim or inspection.

Reports are **confidential**. They hold private details about a client's property, security and weaknesses. Do not share them outside the client's business without permission, and handle personal information as Jamaica's data protection law expects.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the kinds of report used in electrical work and choose the right one for a request.
I can agree a scope with a client and write a clear limitation.
I can record test readings at the time, with units, exactly as the instrument shows them.
I can record an out-of-range reading, a test that was not done, and a circuit that failed and was repaired.
I can explain why instrument serial numbers and calibration dates are recorded.
I can tell a fact from an opinion, and a symptom from a cause.
I can set out a report with a summary, scope, findings, conclusions, recommendations and appendices.
I can class a defect by danger and give the overall result of a condition report.
I can write a location, a reading, a date and a recommendation so that they cannot be misread.
I can choose a table, bar chart, line graph, sketch or photo, and caption it.
I can tally a log and work out percentages correctly.
I can write fault, incident, commissioning, progress and recommendation reports.
I can check a report, control its revisions and sign only for my own part.
I can hand a report over in person, keep it confidential and file it safely.

terms: Appendix
A section at the end of a report for detailed material such as full tables and calculations.
Calibration due date
The date by which a test instrument must next be checked against a known standard.
Commissioning report
A record that new equipment was set up, tested and works as designed.
Condition report
A report on the condition of an existing installation, listing and classing its defects.
Danger present
The class for a defect that puts people at risk now; it must be made safe at once.
Figure
The word used before the number of a drawing, chart or photo in a report.
Improvement recommended
The class for an item that is not dangerous but would make the installation safer if fixed.
Incident
An event at work in which someone was hurt or property was damaged.
Limitations
The section of a report listing what could not be inspected or tested, and why.
Minor works certificate
A certificate for a small addition or change to one existing circuit.
Near miss
An event in which nobody was hurt, but someone could have been.
Recommendations
The part of a report that tells the client what should be done next.
Revision
A numbered, dated new version of a report that replaces an earlier one.
Schedule of test results
The table listing each circuit and its test readings.
Scope
What a report covers, agreed with the client before the work.
Site diary
The daily record of work, visitors, instructions and events on a site.
Summary
A short opening section giving the result, the urgent items and the main recommendation.
Unsatisfactory
The overall result of a condition report when any item is dangerous or potentially dangerous.

c1.title: Inspecting a church hall in Buff Bay
c1.text: Team leader Nadine Brown's team carries out a periodic inspection of a 30-year-old church hall in Buff Bay, Portland. They find: (1) a kitchen outlet with a broken cover and live terminals that can be touched; (2) a metal car-park light at the gate whose earth conductor is disconnected inside the fitting; (3) a circuit chart in the board that is out of date. Of 29 items checked, 26 passed. The church's management committee, none of them electricians, will read the report.

c2.title: A tripping GFCI at a Balaclava cook shop
c2.text: A cook shop in Balaclava, St Elizabeth, complains that the GFCI protecting its kitchen outlets keeps tripping. The owner kept a two-week log of 12 trips: 9 happened between 10 and 11 a.m., one in the afternoon, and 2 have no time written down. Electrician Devon Thompson finds that the sheath of the element in fryer 2 is cracked: its insulation resistance to earth is 0.4 MΩ. He fits a new element, and the retest reads more than 200 MΩ.

c3.title: A fall from a stepladder in Porus
c3.text: On Tuesday 3 November 2026, at about 2:15 p.m., trainee Jordan Clarke fell about 1 m from a stepladder while fitting a ceiling light in Room 2 of a basic school in Porus, Manchester. He grazed his elbow. One rubber foot of the ladder was missing and the floor had just been mopped. The caretaker and another trainee saw the fall. Team leader Sasha-Gaye Morgan must write the incident report.

c4.title: Progress on a supermarket fit-out in Ocho Rios
c4.text: Kemar Wright leads the electrical team fitting out a supermarket in Ocho Rios, St Ann. The plan said the job would be 40% complete at the end of week 3; it is 32% complete. Two days were lost to rain on the roof work, and the client's site representative changed the lighting layout by phone. Kemar's weekly progress report goes to the owner, who reads it on her phone. Last week's report, already issued, gave a wrong delivery date.

c5.title: Test records for a new clinic in Chapelton
c5.text: Apprentice Ricardo Hall, working under supervision, tested 18 new circuits at a clinic in Chapelton, Clarendon, and filled in the schedule of test results. Team leader Gayle Sinclair checks it before it is signed. Circuit 7 has an empty insulation resistance box, because the vaccine fridge it feeds could not be unplugged that day. The RCD result for circuit 15 says only 'ok'.

questions.q: What must Nadine do about the kitchen outlet before her team leaves the hall?
o: Note it for the report she will send next week
Make it safe and tell the church in writing today
Tell the caretaker to keep children away from it
Leave it, as repairs are outside the agreed scope
questions.why: Exposed live parts are 'danger present': people are at risk now. The item is made safe at once, for example by isolating that circuit, and the client is told immediately in writing. Waiting for the finished report could cost a life.

questions.q: Nadine's draft says: 'Overall result: satisfactory, as 26 of 29 items passed.' What is wrong with this?
o: Nothing: 26 of 29 is close to 90%
The result should wait until repairs are done
Only the committee can decide the result
Any dangerous item makes it unsatisfactory
questions.why: The overall result does not depend on a count of passes. One item classed as danger present or potentially dangerous makes the result unsatisfactory, and this hall has both.

questions.q: How should the car-park light be classed?
o: Potentially dangerous: urgent repair needed
Improvement recommended: repair when convenient
Danger present: disconnect the whole hall
No class, since the light still works
questions.why: Nobody is at risk at this moment, but if a fault made the metal body live, there is no earth path to trip the breaker, and the next person to touch it could be shocked. That is 'potentially dangerous' and needs urgent repair.

questions.q: An apprentice's note reads: 'Outside light no good, earth gone.' Which rewrite is best for the report's observations?
o: Outside lighting is in a very poor state and unsafe
Earthing problems were found at the outside lights
Car-park light at gate: earth conductor disconnected
The light at the gate was probably hit by a vehicle once
questions.why: A good observation gives the exact item and the exact fact found. 'Poor state' and 'earthing problems' are vague, and 'probably hit by a vehicle' is an opinion presented as a finding.

questions.q: Which chart best shows the owner when the trips happen?
o: A pie chart of all the insulation readings taken
A bar chart of trips for each hour of the day
A line graph of the supply voltage
A photo of the GFCI with its test button
questions.why: Counting trips for each hour and drawing one bar per hour makes the 10 to 11 a.m. peak obvious at a glance, which points to whatever is switched on at that time.

questions.q: What share of all the logged trips happened between 10 and 11 a.m.?
questions.why: 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75%. The two trips with no time still count in the total of 12; leaving them out (9 ÷ 10) would give a misleading 90%.

questions.q: How should Devon's report treat the two trips that have no time written in the log?
o: Count them, and say their times were not recorded
Leave them out, so that the chart is easier to read
Show them at 10 a.m., the most common time
Ask the owner to guess, and enter the guesses
questions.why: Honest reporting shows the data as it is. The trips happened, so they are counted; their times are unknown, so the report says so. Inventing or dropping data would make the chart look better than the evidence.

questions.q: Which sentence belongs under 'Cause' in the fault report?
o: The GFCI tripped 12 times in two weeks
Replace the element in fryer 2 and retest
Fryer 2's element sheath is cracked and leaks current
The owner lost sales each time the kitchen power went off
questions.why: The cause explains why the fault happens. Twelve trips is the symptom, replacing the element is the repair, and lost sales are the effect on the client.

questions.q: How should Sasha-Gaye collect the accounts of the caretaker and the other trainee?
o: Together, so that their two stories agree
A week later, once everyone has calmed down
By writing down what she thinks they saw
Separately and soon, in their own words
questions.why: Memories fade and people influence each other. Separate statements taken soon after the event, in each person's own words, give the most reliable facts for the report.

questions.q: Which sentence is best for the 'What happened' section?
o: Jordan was not paying attention and fell off
At about 2:15 p.m. Jordan fell 1 m from a stepladder
The ladder was a disgrace and should never have been used
The caretaker caused the fall by mopping the floor
questions.why: The account gives facts in time order: when, who, what, how far. Blame and strong opinions do not belong there; the causes are worked out from the facts, in their own section.

questions.q: Which entry belongs in the report's 'Actions' section?
o: Inspect all stepladders by 6 November: S. Morgan
Jordan to take much more care on ladders in future
Ladders are dangerous and should be avoided
The school should not mop floors during the day
questions.why: A useful action says what will be done, by whom and by when, and deals with a real cause: here, a ladder with a missing foot that was still in use. 'Take more care' changes nothing that can be checked.

questions.q: Which statement about progress is accurate?
o: The job is 8% ahead of the plan
The job is 32 percentage points behind plan
The job is 8 percentage points behind plan
The job is on plan, as 32% is close to 40%
questions.why: Both figures are percentages of the whole job, so subtract them: 40 − 32 = 8 percentage points behind. The report should then give the causes and the effect on the finish date.

questions.q: How should the report deal with the lighting layout that was changed by phone?
o: Leave it out for now, to avoid upsetting the client
Record it and its effect; ask for written approval
Mention it only if the job finishes late
State in bold that the delay is the client's fault
questions.why: A change asked for by word of mouth is recorded as a fact, with its effect on time and cost, and the report asks for it to be confirmed in writing. That protects both sides; blame and silence protect nobody.

questions.q: Which chart best shows the owner planned against actual progress, week by week?
o: A pie chart of all the work still to be done
A table of every cable pulled so far
A photo of the site taken each Friday
A line graph with planned and actual lines
questions.why: Progress is a change over time, so a line graph suits it. Two lines on the same axes, planned and actual, show at once whether the gap is growing or closing.

questions.q: Kemar must reissue last week's report with the delivery date corrected. What should the corrected copy show?
o: A new revision number and date, noting the change
The same number and date, so nothing looks different
No number at all, as it replaces the old file
Only the corrected page, sent without a cover
questions.why: A corrected report gets a new revision number and date and a note of what changed, and goes to everyone who had the first one. Two different reports with the same number lead to arguments about which is right.

questions.q: What should go in the empty insulation resistance box for circuit 7?
o: The reading from circuit 6, which is a similar circuit
'>299 MΩ', because the cable is new
'Not tested', with the reason and a test date
Nothing: a blank shows that it was skipped
questions.why: A blank could mean forgotten, failed or not needed. 'Not tested: vaccine fridge could not be unplugged; test booked for…' tells the truth and makes sure the test is done. A copied or assumed reading is a false record.

questions.q: How should the RCD result for circuit 15 be recorded?
o: As 'ok', since the RCD did trip when it was tested
As the measured trip time, in milliseconds
As 'PASS' in capital letters, with the date beside it
As the RCD's rating, 30 mA
questions.why: A schedule records what was measured, with its unit, for example '24 ms', so that anyone can compare it with the limit. 'Ok' and 'pass' are judgements with no evidence, and 30 mA is the device's rating, not a test result.

questions.q: Ricardo did the tests under supervision. Who signs the inspection and testing part of the certificate?
o: Ricardo alone, since he wrote the readings
The clinic manager, as the person who owns the building
Nobody, until the next periodic inspection
The competent person responsible for the tests
questions.why: A signature accepts responsibility. The competent person who supervised the testing and is responsible for it signs that part; an apprentice's work is signed for by that person.

questions.q: Which is the correct way to write a current of thirty milliamps?
o: 30 mA
30 MA.
30mAs
questions.why: The prefix m (milli) is a small letter and A (ampere) is a capital, with a space after the number and no 's'. 'MA' would mean megaamps: a million amps.

questions.q: A four-page fault report for a shop owner is backed by a table of 60 test readings. Where should the full table go?
o: On the first page, before the summary
In the middle of the findings, in full
In an appendix, with key results in the findings
Nowhere: the readings should stay in the site notebook
questions.why: The main text gives the reader the key results; bulky detail goes in an appendix, where anyone who needs to check it can find it. Leaving the readings out would remove the evidence the report rests on.
